name: Victorian Period (1832–1901)
description: Literature written in British and American English between the first British Reform Act and the death of Queen Victoria. On the British side: the lyric and the long poem of Tennyson, Browning, Arthur Hugh Clough, Matthew Arnold and the Pre-Raphaelites; the serial novel from Dickens through the sensation fiction of the 1860s to the problem fiction of the 1890s; the prose of Carlyle, Ruskin, Newman, Pater and Arnold; and the stage from domestic drama and burlesque to the problem play and Wilde. On the American side: Transcendentalism; the dark romance of Hawthorne and Melville; the poetry of Whitman and Dickinson; the slave narrative and the plantation tradition; the tall tale and the local-colour school; the realist programme of Howells and James; Twain's vernacular; and the naturalism of Crane, Norris and Chopin at the century's close.
historical_context: The period opens with the Great Reform Act (1832) and closes with Victoria's death in January 1901. Between: the New Poor Law (1834); Chartism, the People's Charter of 1838 and the petitions of 1842 and 1848; the Ten Hours Act (1847); the repeal of the Corn Laws (1846); the Second and Third Reform Acts (1867, 1884); the Elementary Education Act (1870); and the rise of organised labour and of the socialist societies of the 1880s. An expanding print economy — railway bookstalls, the weekly and monthly part-issue, the three-volume library, the penny periodical and after 1870 the cheap reissue — creates the first mass reading public, with a rising proportion of women readers and women writers. Empire supplies subject and capital: the Indian Mutiny of 1857–58 and the Crown settlement afterwards, the Crimean War (1854–56), the reconquest of the Sudan (1898), the Diamond and Golden Jubilees (1887, 1897), and after 1884 the East African partition; emigration and the colonial exhibitions make London an imperial city. In the United States: Indian Removal after the 1830 act; the Mexican War (1846–48) and the gold rush of 1849; the Fugitive Slave Law (1850); the Civil War (1861–65), Emancipation and the Reconstruction amendments; the withdrawal of federal troops in 1877 and the loss of Reconstruction; the transcontinental railroad (completed 1869), the great rail and labour conflicts of the 1870s, 1886 and 1894; the census declaration of a settled frontier line in the early 1890s; mass immigration from the 1880s; and the Spanish-American War and the overseas settlements of 1898. International copyright arrangements of the 1890s turn the two literary cultures into one market.
literary_characteristics: A literature of large public prose and of conscience: moral, religious and social argument carried in the quarterly review, the sermon, the lecture and the treatise; a claimed "high seriousness" for poetry after Arnold's phrase, matched by an equally deliberate counter-programme of pleasure, surface and style in aesthetic and decadent writing from the 1860s to the 1890s. Formally: the serial novel with its sustained suspense; the dramatic monologue and the masked lyric; the revived sonnet and the elegiac sequence; the blank-verse tale and the idyll; the problem play and the sensation drama; in America the talk, the sketch, the yarn and the long improvisation of Whitman's free line, answered by Dickinson's compressed stanza. Forms are increasingly named from their publication venue — the magazine story, the part-issue, the recited dialect poem, the "bestseller" — and the period closes with the little magazines and the lyric anthologies that will make the next century's repertoires.
